extracted.intended_audience: Christian lay readers seeking moral and practical instruction on marriage, family life, honesty, and debt
extracted.subtask_short: christian moral instruction on family and debt
extracted.subtask_description: Didactic religious guidance about proper Christian behaviour in marriage, parenting, business honesty, and responses to indebtedness, grounded in Scripture and illustrative examples. The text lists prohibitions, consequences, and practical counsel for believers and their families.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on marrying unbelievers
rubrics_metrics.description: Beleivers are forbidden to marry unbelievers: supported by Old and New Testament commands (Deut. 7:4–5; 'Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text cites Scripture as a clear prohibition and treats such marriages as morally impermissible for the believer. The prohibition is presented as binding and grounded in divine law rather than merely social custom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural-analogy against unequal marriages
rubrics_metrics.description: Unequal/unlawful marriages are contrary to nature—irrational creatures 'will not couple but with their own sort' (e.g., sheep with dogs, partridge with crow).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analogy to animals is used to reinforce the abnormality and impropriety of mixed marriages; the social astonishment at such mixtures is noted as further evidence of their inappropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spiritual dangers and consequences of unequal marriages
rubrics_metrics.description: Such marriages commonly lead to spiritual decline: conviction, prayer, and hungering/thirsting after salvation often cease; spouses are estranged from the Word, godly friends, and drawn into carnal company and delights, resulting in sinful life and possible damnation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provided as causal evidence for the prohibition: specific spiritual steps toward salvation are named as being interrupted (conviction, prayer, hunger for salvation). The practical social outcome—return to carnal company and eventual perdition—is given as an empirical warning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scriptural reason: unbelievers will turn your children from God
rubrics_metrics.description: God forbids unequal marriages because 'they... will turn away thy son from following me, that they may serve other Gods,' invoking divine wrath and historical examples from Israel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text cites Israelite examples where disobedient marriages led to idolatry, child sacrifice, and the wrath of the Lord; this historical precedent is offered as a justification and warning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects on children of mixed (godly/ungodly) parents
rubrics_metrics.description: Children of a godly and an ungodly parent are often divided: some follow the godly parent's ways, some follow the ungodly parent's ways, and some become 'mungrel'—having the mother's notions/words but the father's life/lusts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains parental struggle over children (prayers, counsel, examples vs. counter-instruction), and warns that such children are disadvantaged in both trust and company—they are fit for neither the good nor the bad community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages for children of godly parents
rubrics_metrics.description: Children of godly parents benefit by being the objects of many prayers, restraint from evils, godly instruction about right and wrong, commendation of good ways, protection from bad company and books, and exemplary godly life shown by parents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text lists these specific advantages (prayers before and after birth; restraint; instruction; commendation of good; kept from evil company and books; doctrinal and practical example) and calls them 'very great mercies.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Disadvantages for children of ungodly parents
rubrics_metrics.description: Children of ungodly parents lack prayer and heartfelt instruction, are not restrained from evil, are exposed to Sabbath-breaking, swearing, lying, mockery of good men, and are generally estranged from the love of God and good people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a 'very great Judgment of God' upon such children; the text emphasizes that ungodly parents act contrary to what is needed to raise holy children, thereby increasing danger of the child's ruin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of conscience and soul over spousal commands
rubrics_metrics.description: A believer (example: a wife) must prioritize her duty to God and her soul over her husband's objections—'I have an Husband, but also a God... my Soul ought to be more unto me than all the world besides.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The wife's decision to attend worship despite the husband's threats is upheld; the text argues worship and salvation obligations supersede marital coercion, and resisting such coercion may invite spousal malice but is morally required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Malice and social harassment as characteristic of the ungodly spouse
rubrics_metrics.description: Ungodly spouses may threaten to inform on worshippers, incite others to molest and abuse their spouse's friends, rejoice at misfortunes befalling them, and mock their distress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text describes three concrete behaviors of Mr. Badman (inciting molestation, wishing mischief upon them, laughing at her trouble) to illustrate the malicious social tactics of such men and to warn believers of expected persecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divine judgments on informers and persecutors (cautionary examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: God's judgments may visibly afflict informers and persecutors—examples include progressive speech failure, dribbling/slabbering at the mouth, neck weakness, loss of speech to animal noises, and sudden miserable death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two illustrative cases of informers are narrated (W.S. and a gentleman's man) showing bodily afflictions and death as divine retribution; the narrator frames these true stories as admonitions to fear God and avoid persecuting the godly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemnation of hypocrisy and adaptive wickedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who adapt their speech and behaviour to please different companies—professing religion with some and irreligion with others, boasting of being able to do either—are condemned as atheists/hypocrites and morally culpable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr. Badman is described as skillfully changing persona to suit customers (appearing pious with honest men, obscene with the wicked), taking pride in his ability to sin without remorse; this adaptive wickedness is treated as evidence of a corrupt heart and Atheism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inner desires and intentions are judged as sin
rubrics_metrics.description: Wickedness proceeds from the heart; God judges desires, intentions, and endeavours as well as overt acts—'As he thinketh, so is he' and 'He that looketh upon a woman to lust after her, hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes that people are judged not only for deeds but for their inner inclinations; striving or desiring to be wicked is itself culpable and will be judged accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breaking (deliberate bankruptcy/defrauding creditors) is theft and forbidden
rubrics_metrics.description: The deliberate practice of 'breaking'—contracting debts, collecting goods/money, then absconding or using legal composition to avoid payment—is defrauding, akin to theft and robbery; Scripture forbids 'Thou shalt not defraud thy neighbour, nor rob him.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text details the method (building credit, selling below cost, feathering the nest, confederates, deceitful letters, composition bargains like 'five shillings in the pound') and condemns the premeditated, deceitful nature of the crime; it calls God the avenger and likens the sin to the serpent's beguiling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical counsel for debtors: do not run further into debt if unable to pay
rubrics_metrics.description: If a man knows he cannot pay his creditors and cannot continue trade, he must not run one penny further into debt; knowingly incurring debt one cannot repay is wrongful and falls under 'the wicked borroweth and payeth not again.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is offered as the first concrete remedy: cease creating additional obligations when insolvent. The text frames continuing to borrow under known insolvency as deliberate wronging and conscience-violating behavior.
